source.title: Pretraining and adapting a language model on a dependency-free stack: GPT-2 124M from random weights, reproduced against llm.c, and a clinical adapter for Qwen3-0.6B

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Reports held-out pretraining loss at multiple points along a fixed-size model's token-training trajectory, which bears on the token axis of V1. It does not run the multi-size, multi-budget scaling sweeps used to fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out loss over training steps for one GPT-2 size, in comparisons against two reference runs, plus endpoint losses. It does not fit or test a power-law form. The clinical adapter's loss and the HellaSwag scores are not results about scaling-law shape or prediction. The cited scaling-law findings are background, not results of this study.
record.test_reason: This is a software-engineering reproduction study: one GPT-2 124M run on the numbat stack, compared step by step with llm.c reference runs. Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. are cited only as background on the tokens-per-parameter budget. No result varies parameters, tokens or compute to test loss scaling. Loss over training steps within a single cosine-schedule run is a training curve, not a scaling-law measurement, and no power law is fitted. The log-step interpolation used by the sidecar gate is a design assumption ('loss falls roughly linearly against that'), not a tested result.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that an independent, dependency-free stack can carry a model through pretraining and specialist adaptation and be checked at each stage. Specifically, the 124M GPT-2 reproduces llm.c (3.2588 vs 3.29 loss, 0.3053 vs 0.299 HellaSwag). The one-sided gap is attributed to the 0.195% larger batch, and the reference itself reproduces to 0.0035 across hardware. They explicitly claim no new method and make no scaling-law claim.
record.recipe_differences: The pretraining recipe follows llm.c for one GPT-2 size and one token budget, with a slightly larger per-step batch; it does not reproduce the multi-size scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper attributes the consistent loss gap against the reference to the 0.195% larger token batch per step; the gap narrows over the longer comparison.
record.problems: Only one model size and one pretraining run are used; no power-law fit, exponents, or scaling sweeps are reported. Same-machine reference coverage ends at step 2,000, and the paper notes the batch-size difference was not isolated.
record.rows_left_out: No results relevant to the listed scaling-law versions were left out. Clinical adaptation losses and HellaSwag endpoint scores were not extracted because they do not test scaling-law shape or predictability.

untested.parts: All parts. There is one model size and one token budget. Loss is never varied against parameters, tokens or compute, and no power law is fitted.
All parts. No small-run fit is extrapolated to larger runs.
All parts. No compute-optimal allocation sweep is run. The 80 tokens/param versus Chinchilla's ~20 comparison is background only.
All parts. Only one architecture is used.
All parts. The single LoRA clinical run gives no scaling form.
All parts. HellaSwag is reported only at endpoints of a single model size.
All parts. No exponents or fitting choices are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 with V1 links is wrong. All 35 rows are framework-vs-reference comparisons of one fixed-size run and should carry versions ['none']. Scaling-law papers appear only in the Background paragraph on token budget.

versions.untested_parts: Only loss over training steps for one fixed-size pretraining run is measured. The paper does not test loss scaling with parameter count or compute, fit a power law in tokens, report exponents, or test the claim across several model sizes.
No small-run fit is used to predict a much larger run.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
No architecture comparison at fixed parameter count is reported.
The clinical adapter is a single fine-tuning run, not a test of power-law form across training regimes or modalities.
The paper reports endpoint HellaSwag scores but does not test downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or curve departures from power laws is made.
